chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to me: Ibrahim ibn Maymun said to me, 'I was sitting in the presence of Abu Hanifa when a man came to him and asked him. He said: 'What do you think regarding a man who has performed the Hajj of Islam (the obligatory one)? Is the Hajj superior or freeing a neck (slave)?' He said: 'No, rather freeing a neck.' So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'He lied, by Allah, and sinned! A Hajj is superior to freeing a neck, and a neck, and a neck,' until he counted ten.

Then he said: 'Woe be unto him! In which neck are the circumambulation of the House, and the Sa'i between Al-Safa and Al-Marwa, and the standing at Arafat, and the shaving of the head, and the pelting of the Jamarat? If it were as he said, people would have suspended the Hajj. And if they had done so, it would have been befitting for the Imam to compel them upon the Hajj, whether they wish it or refuse, for this House was placed only for the Hajj.'
ai.seo_question: Is performing Hajj superior to freeing a slave according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi highlights the Shia scholarly preference for the obligatory Hajj over the voluntary act of manumission, explicitly countering the Hanafi jurist Abu Hanifa’s view that freeing a slave holds greater merit. Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) emphasizes the unique, irreplaceable nature of Hajj rituals—such as Tawaf and Wuquf at Arafah—arguing that their specific divine purpose justifies making them compulsory for the community, even by force if necessary, to preserve the sanctity of the Kaaba.
